name: A/B Street (abstreet) and osm2streets
type: simulator (A/B Street: agent-based traffic simulator and street editor) plus library (osm2streets: OSM-to-lane-level street geometry)
maintainer: Dustin Carlino and contributors, now A/B Street Ltd (abstreet.uk); repositories under github.com/a-b-street
first_release: A/B Street repository created June 2018; osm2streets repository created May 2022; osm2lanes created Nov 2021 and archived Mar 2023
last_activity: abstreet: last commit 2025-09-10 (README points to successor projects; last packaged release v0.3.49). osm2streets: last commit 2025-10-02 ('Update git dependencies'). osm2streets-js on npm: latest 0.1.4 published 2023-06-04. osm2lanes: archived, last commit 2023-03-09
licence: Apache-2.0 for abstreet, osm2streets, osm2streets-js (npm) and osm2lanes
language: Rust core; compiled to WebAssembly for the browser via wasm-bindgen; osm2streets also has JavaScript (osm2streets-js), Python (osm2streets-py) and in-progress Java bindings; StreetExplorer web UI uses Svelte/TypeScript
code_availability: Source: https://github.com/a-b-street/abstreet and https://github.com/a-b-street/osm2streets ; browser build at https://play.abstreet.org/0.3.49/abstreet.html ; npm package osm2streets-js
maintenance_health: abstreet is not archived but is effectively in maintenance mode: the README '2025 Update' says the project 'has turned into several others' (Network Planning Workspace, LTN tool, 15-minute tool, od2net) and recent commits are dependency bumps and link fixes. The traffic simulation is not where effort goes any more; the retrospective says 'nobody's using it'. osm2streets still receives small commits (2025), has 160 stars and about 33 open issues, but the README warns the API is not stable, and the npm package has not been republished since June 2023, so the npm build drifts behind main. osm2lanes is archived.
scale: Microscopic agent-based, but discrete-event rather than time-stepped (agents schedule their next state transition in a priority queue)
car_following: No continuous car-following model. Vehicles change speed instantly ('no smooth acceleration from rest, or modeling of safe stopping distance'); followers are bounded by the leader position plus vehicle length and a fixed FOLLOWING_DISTANCE of 1.0 m. Vehicle lengths in code: car 4.5-6.5 m, bus 12.5 m, bike 1.8 m.
lane_model: Strict lane-based. Lanes are inferred from OSM tags (lanes, turn:lanes, cycleway, parking etc.) and listed left-to-right with type, direction and width. Lane changes happen mainly at intersections via turns; there is a limited discretionary overtaking lane change with a 'ghost' left in the original lane. Mandatory mid-block lane changing was attempted and removed because 'many vehicles repeatedly attempted lane-changing maneuvers required by pathfinding'.
lateral_model_type: None (lane-based only; no sublane or continuous lateral position)
junction_model: Intersections are polygons built by thickening road centre-lines by inferred width, trimming roads back where thickened edges collide, and joining the points clockwise into a polygon. Turns between lanes are inferred, honouring OSM turn restrictions. Control types: uncontrolled, stop sign (signed), traffic signal, construction (osm2streets IntersectionControl). Conflicts are resolved per turn; vehicles cross one at a time; 'block-the-box' protection stops a vehicle entering a junction it cannot clear; 'uber-turns' lock a sequence of turns through a cluster of nearby intersections and synchronise signal groups. Short dual-carriageway segments are consolidated into one logical intersection (heuristic or manual junction=intersection tag). osm2streets reuses this geometry and adds transforms: collapsing degenerate two-road intersections, merging dog-leg intersections, merging 'sausage links' and dual carriageways. Turning movements and crosswalks are still listed as planned in osm2streets.
signal_control_modes: Fixed-time stages (StageType::Fixed) and a simple demand-responsive/actuated stage (StageType::Variable with minimum, no-demand delay and extension). Signal timing and stages are editable in the UI and via the headless API (/traffic-signals/set). No adaptive or learned-control hooks beyond the HTTP API.
flyover_support: Partial and implicit. Grade separation works only because OSM bridges do not share nodes with the roads below, so no intersection is created where they cross. Motorway on/off-ramps are a documented problem case for intersection geometry. No explicit flyover, ramp-merge or weaving model.
grade_separation_handling: osm2streets reads the OSM 'layer' tag into Road.layer (0 default, negative below), writes it to GeoJSON output for z-ordered rendering, and refuses to collapse an intersection between two roads on different layers (collapse_intersections.rs). There is no elevation model and no check or repair of broken bridge topology. The intersection-geometry docs say outright 'Let's ignore bridges and tunnels', a code comment in block.rs says 'Incorrect near bridges/tunnels', and the retrospective shows gridlock spreading 'from one broken Fremont bridge'.
vehicle_types: Car, Bus, Train, Bike (sim VehicleType enum) plus pedestrians. There are no two-wheelers, auto-rickshaws or trucks as separate motorised classes; bikes are the only small vehicle.
gridlock_policy: Prevention, not resolution: block-the-box protection with a manual override list, uber-turns, a cycle detector, and debugging flags (--disable_turn_conflicts, --disable_block_the_box, --infinite_parking). Scenario modifiers can cancel a share of trips. No teleporting, no dynamic rerouting, and the 'last resort' of releasing a vehicle after a long wait is not implemented. Stuck agents are visible and the 'blocked-by' graph can be queried via the API. The authors admit that 'in most simulations on larger maps, vehicles get stuck. Like, permanently.'
mixed_traffic_support: No. Strict lane discipline, one vehicle per lane slot, fixed 1 m gap; bikes use bike lanes or occupy a whole lane.
non_lane_behaviour: Not supported. There is no lateral position, so vehicles cannot share a lane side by side, form ad hoc columns or ignore markings. Adding this would mean rewriting the core queue-based movement model.
seepage_filtering_support: No. Queues are FIFO per lane; small vehicles cannot move to the front of a queue.
per_class_parameters: Only hard-coded lengths (car 4.5-6.5 m, bus 12.5 m, bike 1.8 m), a 1.0 m following distance and per-agent max speed. No published Indian per-class parameters.
indian_calibration_evidence: [uncertain] No study calibrating or validating A/B Street on Indian traffic was found. A Pune map config exists (importer/config/in/pune), which shows the import runs on an Indian city, not that the behaviour matches Indian traffic.
calibration_dataset_used: [uncertain] None found for India. Seattle uses the PSRC Soundcast demand model; the UK uses census origin-destination flow data.
calibration_method: [uncertain] No formal calibration documented; correctness is checked with regression and screenshot-diff tests on imported maps.
validation_against_field_case: [uncertain] None reported for any Indian location.
network_import: OSM only, via the pipeline: clip the extract with osmium -> convert_osm builds a RawMap -> map_model builds the final Map (since 2022 the shared part lives in osm2streets: lanes from tags, intersection geometry, transforms). osm2streets-js takes OSM XML input plus an optional clip polygon and import options, including override_driving_side, so it works for left-hand-traffic India, and returns GeoJSON (plain network, lane polygons, lane markings, intersection markings) or JSON. Map JSON can be dumped and re-imported (cli dump-json / import-json-map).
demand_input_formats: Scenario files (people and trips, each with start, end, departure time and mode: walk/bike/drive/transit; endpoints are buildings or border intersections). Generators: 'proletariat robot' (home-to-work from OSM building tags, no local data needed), census-based (global population_areas file), UK origin-destination desire lines, Grid2Demand input_agents.csv import, and the abstr R package. Scenario JSON can be dumped, edited and re-run.
data_access: OSM data (ODbL) via Geofabrik or Overpass; A/B Street hosts pre-imported city maps for its own app. No Indian demand data ships with it.
runs_in_browser_or_server: Both: full simulator runs natively (Windows/Mac/Linux) and in the browser as WebAssembly (play.abstreet.org); a 'headless' server mode exposes JSON over HTTP. osm2streets runs in browser (WASM), native Rust or Python.
wasm_or_streaming_feasibility: Proven WASM: both the simulator and osm2streets compile to WebAssembly and run client-side with no server. Caveats from the retrospective: one large WASM bundle 'didn't scale' and had to be split into per-city downloads, and detangling native-only dependencies was 'quite tough'. osm2streets-js is the most reusable piece: an npm package (Apache-2.0) with a JsStreetNetwork constructor and toGeojsonPlain / toLanePolygonsGeojson / toLaneMarkingsGeojson / toIntersectionMarkingsGeojson / toJson methods.
api: A/B Street headless JSON-over-HTTP API (marked 'under construction', no backwards-compatibility guarantees): /sim/load, /sim/goto-time, /sim/new-person, /traffic-signals/get|set|get-delays|get-cumulative-thruput, /data/get-finished-trips|get-agent-positions|get-road-thruput|get-blocked-by-graph, /map/get-all-geometry|get-edits. It holds one map and one sim per server process and serialises requests. osm2streets: Rust crate, JS/WASM (osm2streets-js) and Python bindings.
performance: [uncertain] No published vehicle-count or real-time-factor benchmark was found. The discrete-event design is meant to skip fixed 0.1 s ticks; the docs say the laggy-head retry policy 'will slow down the simulation as traffic jams start to form'.
gpu_requirement: None for simulation; the native and WASM UI need WebGL/OpenGL for rendering.
multi_tenancy_model: Client-side in the browser (zero server cost per user, static hosting). The headless server is single-tenant: one map and sim per process, with requests serialised.
build_complexity: High for the full simulator: a large Rust workspace (8,400+ commits), a city import pipeline and per-city data files. Moderate-low for osm2streets-js: npm install osm2streets-js (0.1.4, 2023) or build from main with wasm-pack and release_npm.sh. The npm build is stale relative to main.
scenario_editability: In A/B Street: lane types (driving, bike, bus, parking, sidewalk), direction, speed limits, road and intersection closures, stop sign versus signal, and signal stages and timing; edits can be exported and re-applied. [uncertain] Lane width editing in the main simulator UI not confirmed. osm2streets has no editing API yet; 'robustly representing user-created edits' is listed as planned.
output_metrics_supported: Trip durations and before/after-edit comparisons, finished trips per mode, intersection delays, cumulative signal throughput, road throughput, live agent positions, and the blocked-by graph. No level of service, PCU, conflict or emissions output.
emissions_support: [uncertain] No emissions model found in the docs or API.
reuse_mode: osm2streets: use as a data/geometry library (OSM -> lane polygons and intersection polygons as GeoJSON) in the browser. A/B Street simulator: inspiration and model to learn from (discrete-event design, uber-turns, block-the-box, gridlock lessons), not as an engine for Indian mixed traffic.
effort_within_72_hours: osm2streets-js: about 2-4 hours to load an OSM extract (Overpass XML) of an Indian junction or corridor in the browser and render lane and intersection polygons on a map; budget extra time for wrong lane counts and widths where OSM lacks lanes/width tags (common in India) and for flyovers whose layer tags are missing. Forking the A/B Street simulator to add mixed, non-lane traffic is not realistic in 72 hours (it would need a new lateral movement model); cut it. Using A/B Street unmodified as the engine is possible but gives lane-disciplined Western behaviour and a large Rust codebase to embed.
licence_constraint: Apache-2.0: permissive. Commercial or closed use is allowed; keep the licence and NOTICE files, state changes, and note the patent-grant termination clause. No copyleft obligation on our code. OSM-derived data stays under ODbL (attribution, share-alike on derived databases).
known_limitations: No acceleration or kinematics; limited lane changing ('one of the main limitations'); gridlock on large maps; bridges and tunnels ignored in geometry; highway ramps produce bad geometry; short roads are 'a currently unsolved problem'; output depends on OSM tag quality (turn lanes often wrong, signal timing not public); headless API unstable; osm2streets API unstable, with turning movements and crosswalks not implemented; no non-lane or mixed traffic; the simulator is no longer the maintainers' focus.
documented_failures: (1) Permanent gridlock in most large-map runs, caused by broken intersection geometry, cautious vehicles, poor signal timing and bad demand data; fixes gave 'only very modest success'. (2) Mandatory lane-changing was removed because agents repeatedly attempted manoeuvres they could not complete. (3) One broken bridge (Fremont, Seattle) spread gridlock across the network. (4) A single WASM blob holding all maps did not scale. (5) Re-importing about 130 maps from about 80 cities was hard to keep up. (6) Self-funded with few users of the simulator; the author calls not forming a business 'likely a mistake'.
validation_approach: Regression tests and screenshot diffs on imported maps (the author calls formal invariants 'pretty impossible targets'); osm2streets has a test suite of tricky real-world junctions (e.g. i5_exit_ramp, montlake_roundabout, taipei, perth_peanut_roundabout, frederiksted) with expected GeoJSON output; the StreetExplorer web app is used for visual checking. No empirical traffic-flow validation was found.
takeaway_for_our_build: Use osm2streets-js (Apache-2.0, WASM) as the OSM-to-geometry front end and visual base layer, but treat its output as a draft that the user can correct, because Indian OSM data often lacks lanes, width and layer tags. Keep the network model separate from the movement model. Do not inherit A/B Street's lane-queue movement model, which cannot represent Indian non-lane traffic. Design gridlock handling up front: detect it, report it and offer a release valve (teleport or timeout), because A/B Street shows that prevention alone fails on real networks. Treat flyovers explicitly: use the OSM layer/bridge tags plus no-shared-node topology, and validate that a road with layer!=0 never forms an at-grade junction with a layer-0 road. Ship a small, curated set of pre-imported scenarios (one or two Indian junctions), not a global importer, to avoid A/B Street's per-city maintenance burden and bundle-size problems.
